```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# readr rather than datawizard::data_read(), which reads empty cells as "" rather than NA
analysts <- readr::read_csv("data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                         col_types = readr::cols(stat_type = readr::col_character()))
ess <- readr::read_csv("data/trust_ess.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

fmt <- \(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
big <- \(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
an <- \(id, col) analysts[[col]][analysts$id == id]

ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
n_paper <- sum(ess$citizen %in% 1 & ess$minority %in% 0)
# the specification of the course closest to the model of 6U3LL, which the
# browser lab reads from the curve beside the reproduction
analogue <- curve |>
  datawizard::data_filter(outcome == "parliament", controls == "paper", weights == "none",
                          items == "available", fe == "country_round")
```

This page sets out the whole exercise of the course on the immigration-and-trust case. The [case study](index.qmd) presents the original study, the SCORE reproductions and replications and the five Multi100 reanalyses, and it is the place to start if you have not read it. Your work happens in the workspace that you downloaded and opened in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), as the [Setup page](../../setup.qmd) describes. The [browser lab](lab.qmd) is a demonstration of the same exercise in a browser tab: it fits no model, and shows every result as the course pipeline computed it with the code of the workspace, beside that code, so it gives the same numbers. It serves for following a demonstration and for submitting to the class chart if your machine fails; to fit a specification yourself, use the workspace. The page of your track gives the timing of each task.

---

## The claim

Five independent analysts reanalysed one claim of the original author (OA) in the Multi100 project [@McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope]. The claim, as the analysts received it, was:

> "... concerns about the effect of immigration on the national community have a(n) \[reducing\] impact on trust in politics" (p. 199)

The published result behind it is the coefficient of concern about immigration in a three-level model of distrust of parliament, with a long list of controls: **0.17 points of distrust per point of concern, with a standard error printed as 0.00**, on 110,732 respondents of the European Social Survey (ESS) in 16 countries, 2002–2009. Both scales run from 0 to 10, so the coefficient says how much more a respondent distrusts parliament, on average, for each additional point of concern, among respondents who are alike on the controls. The data are `r big(nrow(ess))` respondents of the first four rounds of the ESS, `r big(n_paper)` of whom are the citizens who do not belong to an ethnic minority whom the paper analyses.

Your first job is to reproduce the value that Multi100 recorded for one of the analysts, from the file that the analysts received. Your second is to depart from it deliberately, with a written reason, and to find out what that does to the estimate.

## The five Multi100 analysts

```{r}
#| label: tbl-five
#| tbl-cap: "The five reanalyses, with the statistic that Multi100 recorded and the coefficient of the course refit, in points of distrust per point of concern. Source: `data/analysts5.csv`."
#| echo: false
analysts |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Analyst = id,
    Concern = concern,
    Model = method,
    `Recorded statistic` = paste(statistic_type, "=", formatC(statistic_recorded, format = "fg", digits = 6)),
    Respondents = big(n_refit),
    Coefficient = fmt(b_refit, 3)
  ) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 5:6, align = "r")
```

All five found that respondents who are more concerned about immigration distrust parliament more, all five concluded in Task 1 of Multi100 that the data showed evidence for the claim, and the course refits reproduce four of the recorded statistics exactly. Their coefficients still run from `r fmt(min(analysts$b_refit), 3)` to `r fmt(max(analysts$b_refit), 3)`, a factor of about two, because the analysts held constant different lists of controls and one of them measured concern with a single item. The [case study](index.qmd#sec-reanalysts) sets out what each of them chose.

---

## The tasks

The exercise runs as five numbered tasks. Each says what to do in the workspace and, where it differs, in the browser lab.

### Task 1 – The setup check

The only aim is to reach the point where a line of R runs and the data are in front of you. *Workspace:* open the workspace folder in your IDE and run `source("R/check_setup.R")`, which prints OK when everything is in place and otherwise says what is missing. Its last check fits the reference specification of the course, which must come out at `r fmt(ref$b, 4)` points of distrust per point of concern. While you are online, also run `source("R/spec_tools.R"); fetch_multi100()` once, which downloads the file of Task 3. *Browser lab:* wait for the engine and the tables of the course to finish downloading, then run the setup cell, which reads two of them. If your installation will not cooperate, you can follow every later task in the browser lab and still send both results to the class chart, but you cannot fit a specification of your own there.

### Task 2 – The data, the estimand and the graph

First, meet the data in `trust_ess.csv` ([codebook](data/trust_ess_codebook.md)): count the respondents, the countries and the country-rounds, and the respondents of the paper; check how well the three immigration items hang together as one scale; and compare the association of concern with distrust between countries with the association within them.

Second, write the **estimand statement** behind the claim. It says whose distrust is compared, which institution it concerns, how concern is measured and what the comparison holds constant. The [specification menu](menu.qmd#estimand) gives the template.

Third, finish the **causal graph**. Age, sex, education and income, a pessimistic outlook and political ideology can each shape both concern about immigration and distrust of politics, which makes them possible confounders. A vote for a far-right party and the verdicts on the economy and on public services may follow from concern, from distrust or from both. The graph shows which of these the comparison should hold constant, and why holding constant all the controls of the paper can open paths that were closed. It also shows what no set of controls can do, which is to tell an effect of concern on distrust from an effect of distrust on concern, the doubt that analyst FQ1G7 raised. The workspace asks dagitty, the R package for causal graphs, and draws the graph with tinyplot. dagitty cannot run in a browser tab, so the browser lab prints the answers that dagitty gives for every graph that its cell offers, read from a table that the course computed with dagitty.

### Task 3 – The reproduction

Reproduce the value that Multi100 recorded for analyst 6U3LL, **t = `r fmt(an("6U3LL", "statistic_recorded"), 3)` on `r big(an("6U3LL", "n_recorded"))` respondents**, from the file that Multi100 gave the analysts, the file that the SCORE reproduction osf.io/e48gd built from the ESS. *Workspace:* `fetch_multi100()` downloads the file from the OSF into `data_private/` (29 MB) and checks it against its MD5 sum; the file holds person-level survey data, so the workspace does not ship it, and git leaves the folder out. Fit the model of Table 3 of the paper without the unemployment rate, a three-level model with random intercepts for countries and country-rounds, with `lme4::lmer()`. When the facilitator says so, the whole class types its *t* and sends it at the same moment. *Optional extension:* reproduce N8P2J, the full model of Table 3, t = 42.148 on `r big(an("N8P2J", "n_refit"))` respondents, and find out why it loses the Swiss respondents.

Then find out what the number depends on. An intercept for every country-round in place of the random intercepts gives almost the same coefficient on the same file, so the model is not what matters. The same specification on the course extract gives `r fmt(analogue$b, 3)` on `r big(analogue$n)` respondents against `r fmt(an("6U3LL", "b_refit"), 3)` on the file of the analysts, because the two files code several variables differently, the vote controls among them, as the [case study](index.qmd#sec-analyst-file) explains. *Browser lab:* the OSF does not give a page on another website permission to read the file, and the course cannot host a copy of its own, so the lab shows the reproduction as the course pipeline computed it with the code of the workspace, beside that code, and reads the analogue on the course extract from the curve.

### Task 4 – The menu

This task is **exploratory**. `try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), and each defaults to the reference specification: distrust of parliament, the controls of the paper, no weights, every item of a scale answered, and an intercept for every country-round. Five decisions vary on the curve, `outcome`, `controls`, `weights`, `items` and `fe`, so changing one thing means changing one argument. Try several specifications, one decision at a time, and note which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. An option that is not on the curve, such as `concern = "culture"` or `fe = "random_intercepts"`, is refused with the reason given in `menu_options.csv` and the page that teaches it. `my_experiments()` prints everything that you have tried side by side. Then choose the specification that you would defend, and `submit_exploration()` sends it to the class chart on the [multiverse page](multiverse.qmd), where it appears as an open circle.

Nothing in this task is preregistered. You may look, change your mind and try again, and the chart marks the result as exploratory for that reason.

### Task 5 – Declaration and report

Choose **one** specification, one option for each of the twelve decisions, and complete the preregistration block **before you run it**: the claim, your option for each decision, and a sentence, grounded in your causal graph, on why the specification answers the claim. `prereg()` checks the choices and prints the block with your estimand statement. `run_spec()` fits the specification that you declared, and `report_result()` sends the declared result to the class chart, where it appears as a filled circle. Then find where your result sits on the curve of `r nrow(curve)` specifications.

Task 4 and Task 5 run the same code. An exploratory specification can have been chosen because of its result and a declared one cannot, and you submit both so that the two sets of class results can be compared.

---

## What counts as a result

A result counts for the class chart if it is one of the `r nrow(curve)` specifications on the curve, if it reaches the chart through `submit_exploration()` or `report_result()`, which fill in the class-results form for you, and if it comes with a written reason for each choice; two sentences are enough. On this claim every specification of the curve gives a coefficient above zero that is significant at the 5% level, so the class results will differ in size rather than in verdict. The reasons are what show which differences come from asking different questions, above all from holding different things constant, and which from different ways of answering the same one.
